# Maṅgala Sutta (Snp 2.4 (PTS Snp 46))

**ID:** Snp 2.4 (PTS Snp 46)
**Section:** Suttanipāta (snp)
**Collection:** Sutta
**Title (Pali):** Maṅgala Sutta
**tipitaka.org (CST):** https://tipitaka.org/romn/cscd/s0505m.mul1.xml

## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature)

*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and catalog data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*

The *Maṅgala Sutta* (also known as the *Mahāmaṅgala Sutta*) is the fourth discourse of the Cūḷavagga in the *Suttanipāta* [Buswell & Lopez 2014; Winternitz 1933]. Introduced by a prose preface in which an inquiring deity requests the Buddha to explain what constitutes the highest blessing (*maṅgala*), the text consists of twelve verses outlining a progressive path of skillful conduct and social virtues [Powers 2016; Buswell & Lopez 2014]. These blessings range from everyday social and domestic foundations—such as avoiding fools, associating with the wise, revering parents, caring for spouse and children, blameless livelihoods, and abstaining from intoxicants—to emotional stability in the face of worldly conditions (*phuṭṭhassa lokadhammehi*) and the realization of *nibbāna* [Buswell & Lopez 2014; Walker, Unfolding Buddhism].

Celebrated as one of the most widely recited discourses in the Theravāda world, the sutta holds a preeminent place in the *paritta* (protective chant) collection [Powers 2016; Buswell & Lopez 2014]. It long formed an essential curricular text for early monastic and lay literacy, notably in Burma where it was memorized by young students [Turner 2009]. In sixteenth-century Chiang Mai, the scholar-monk Sirimaṅgala composed the *Maṅgalatthadīpanī*, a monumental Pali commentary on the sutta that greatly expanded on obligations to parents and the practice of giving (*dāna*); this commentary remains a central fixture of monastic education in Thailand [von Hinüber 1996; Heim 2004; Walker, Unfolding Buddhism].

**Sources**

- [Buswell & Lopez 2014] Robert E. Buswell Jr. & Donald S. Lopez Jr., Princeton Dictionary of Buddhism (2014) — Structure of twelve verses, summary of virtues, paritta status, and overview of the Mangalatthadīpanī.
- [Powers 2016] John Powers, ed., The Buddhist World (2016) — Twelve-verse structure, protective ritual chanting, and concept of maṅgala.
- [Winternitz 1933] Maurice Winternitz, A History of Indian Literature, Vol. II (1933) — Canonical presence in both Khuddakapāṭha and Suttanipāta, and citation in Jātaka commentary.
- [Turner 2009] Alicia Marie Turner, Buddhism, Colonialism and the Boundaries of Religion (2009) — Role of the sutta in traditional Burmese early education curricula.
- [von Hinüber 1996] Oskar von Hinüber, A Handbook of Pāli Literature (1996) — Details on Sirimaṅgala composing the Mangalatthadīpanī in Chiang Mai.
- [Heim 2004] Maria Heim, Theories of the Gift in South Asia (2004) — Significance of Mangalatthadīpanī's chapter on dāna and core status in modern Thai monastic training.
- [Walker, Unfolding Buddhism] Trent Walker, Unfolding Buddhism — Quotation of verse half-line phuṭṭhassa lokadhammehi and commentarial expansion on filial gratitude in Southeast Asia.
- [Anālayo 2018] Bhikkhu Anālayo, Rebirth in Early Buddhism and Current Research (2018) — Dual occurrence of the sutta in the Khuddakapāṭha and Sutta-nipāta.
- [Gaffney 2003] Sean D. Gaffney, The Jātakanidānakathā: A Critical Study (2003) — Identification of the Tibetan Kangyur translation of the Mahāmaṅgala-sutta produced with Ceylon paṇḍita Ānandaśrī.
